analysis.one_liner: Cuts self-employment taxes for owners earning under $400,000, paid for by taxing corporate stock buybacks.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote; it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee from July 2022 until the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let self-employed people who earn less than $400,000 a year deduct three-quarters of their payroll (self-employment) taxes instead of the current half, trimming their tax bill. To pay for it, the bill would charge publicly traded companies a 0.8% tax on the value of their own stock that they buy back from shareholders. It was referred to the tax-writing committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Self-employed small business owners earning under $400,000 a year — freelancers, contractors, and owner-operators — who would keep more of the payroll taxes they pay. The federal treasury would come out roughly even, because the buyback tax is designed to cover the cost.

how_it_helps.text: Self-employed taxpayers with gross income under $400,000 could deduct three-quarters of their payroll taxes instead of the current one-half, reducing their income tax bill.

The cost would be offset by a 0.8% excise tax on the fair market value of stock that publicly traded domestic corporations buy back, with an exception for repurchases of $1 million or less per year and for stock redirected to employee retirement plans.
The bill counts employee stock issuances and certain affiliate purchases as repurchases and directs the Treasury to write rules preventing avoidance, so companies could not easily sidestep the tax.

analysis.who_pays: Large publicly traded corporations that repurchase their own stock, and to some extent their shareholders, who would bear a 0.8% tax on buybacks.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large public companies buying back stock

drawbacks.text: The deduction is generous up to a very high income level: a self-employed person earning $399,999 qualifies for the same enhanced deduction as one earning $60,000, so much of the benefit goes to relatively high earners rather than struggling small businesses.

A buyback tax is ultimately paid by shareholders, which includes retirement funds and pension accounts holding stock on behalf of ordinary savers, and companies might respond by shifting cash toward dividends instead.
Companies would face compliance costs in tracking repurchases, affiliate acquisitions, and stock issuances under the new rules the bill directs Treasury to write.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade is reasonable on its face: a targeted tax cut for self-employed workers paid for by a modest levy on corporate buybacks, with the $1 million exception sparing small issuers. The main design flaw is the $400,000 income ceiling, which directs part of the benefit to comfortably high earners. The buyback tax is small enough that its effect on retirement savers or corporate investment would be limited.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Angie Craig introduced the bill on July 28, 2022, pairing a larger payroll-tax deduction for lower- and middle-income self-employed people with a 0.8% excise tax on corporate stock buybacks to cover the cost.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation.
No further action was ever taken: the committee never scheduled a hearing or a vote, no vote ever occurred in the House or Senate, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
One House Democrat cosponsored the bill; no other support was recorded.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large publicly traded companies avoided the 0.8% buyback tax, and self-employed small business owners got no tax relief. Congress's taxwriters were unburdened of either decision.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large companies that buy back stock

for.name: Rep. Angie Craig
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill pairing self-employment tax relief with a stock buyback tax.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax bills
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored and cosponsored only by House Democrats, with no Republican cosponsor recorded, and it never advanced far enough to reveal how either party's members would have voted.

industries.note: The bill would tax their stock buybacks at 0.8% of the repurchased shares' value, a direct new cost. Their interest in blocking it ran against the bill's funding of a tax cut for self-employed workers.

Owners earning under $400,000 would deduct three-quarters of their payroll taxes instead of half, keeping more of their income. This group includes freelancers and owner-operators, not a concentrated industry.
